title: A Pro-ICE Sheriff, Once Investigated for Racist Slurs, Is Ousted in North Carolina
author: Jacob Biba
content:
On Tuesday, a Black pastor who campaigned against racial profiling and
eliminating the [“good ol’ boy
system”](https://www.newsoforange.com/community/article_66f5a8dd-7e88-47ef-b680-537e203726b8.html)
of policing ousted six-term North Carolina Sheriff Terry Johnson, an Alamance
County Republican who has faced accusations of racism and illegal policing
tactics throughout his time in office.

Shannon Long, a former school resource officer who now runs a local Christian
ministry and barber school, ran as an unaffiliated candidate and defeated
Johnson by nearly 5 percentage points, or more than 3,100 votes. A reliable
Republican stronghold before Tuesday, Alamance County also saw its county
board of commissioners and district attorney’s office
[flip](https://alamancenews.com/details-democrats-blue-wave-sweeps-
republicans-out-of-sheriffs-and-d-a-s-offices-commissioner-board-state-house/)
for Democrats.

For years Johnson has faced accusations of targeting Latino residents in
traffic stops and referring to them with racist epithets such as “taco
eaters.” In 2012, the U.S. Department of Justice investigated Johnson [and
accused
him](https://www.justice.gov/iso/opa/resources/171201291812462488198.pdf) of
fostering “a culture of discrimination against Latinos.”

He has also faced complaints of excessive force, including when his office
[countered Black Lives Matters
protestors](https://www.propublica.org/article/small-town-battle-for-racial-
justice-confronts-bloody-past-uncertain-future) with violence in 2020.

Maria Mejia, who immigrated to the U.S. from Colombia in 2001 and moved to
Alamance County three years ago, told _Bolts_ that Johnson’s actions in
office—from partnering with ICE in 2007 to setting up checkpoints outside
Latino neighborhoods—has made the sheriff a “fearsome figure” in the
community. Mejia, who works as an assistant professor of philosophy at Elon
University, near Burlington, Alamance County’s most populous city, has worked
with the immigrant rights group Siembra NC to provide ICE verification
training to community members.

“These very valid feelings of anger and distrust have been present for so long
in the community, and yet Johnson continued to get reelected over and over
again,” Mejia said. “I think it was extremely demoralizing for the community.”

Johnson’s ouster, Mejia added, will “give people a sense that they have a
voice, that it's not just the good ol’ boys club, but that they can enact
change.”

Johnson has long partnered with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, first as
an early participant of the agency’s 287(g) program, which empowered his
deputies to interrogate people about immigration status while out on patrols.
He also leased jail space to ICE to hold immigrant detainees.

Johnson
[ended](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/immigration/alamance-
county-terry-johnson-sheriff-ice/) that ICE detention agreement last year and
previously told _Bolts_ the sheriff’s office no longer participates in 287(g),
though Alamance County remains on ICE’s database of counties with an active
287(g) contract.

Federal immigration authorities routinely contract with local law enforcement
agencies to grow their reach, which means that sheriff and police departments
are crucial allies. On Tuesday, voters ousted other sheriffs who’ve closely
worked with ICE, such as Maryland’s Chuck Jenkins, a [notorious far-
right](https://boltsmag.org/voters-oust-notorious-pro-ice-sheriff-in-
maryland/) sheriff in office for two decades. Jenkins got his county in the
outskirts of Washington, D.C., to join ICE’s 287(g) program back in 2008, just
one year after Alamance.

The Trump administration has signaled it is undeterred by the results, saying
on Wednesday that “[deportations will
continue](https://x.com/SecMullinDHS/status/2118064490789097730).”

Johnson has long denied that he racially profiled residents in Alamance
County, where he’s been sheriff for more than 20 years. Asked about the
accusations in May, Johnson told _Bolts_ , “Yeah, we profile—we profile
criminals. I don’t care if you’re Black, white, short, tall, fat, small,
Democrat, Republican, independent. If you’re a criminal, we coming after you.”

Johnson did not respond to a request for comment sent through a sheriff’s
office spokesperson. In a [statement](https://myfox8.com/news/north-
carolina/alamance/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-releases-statement-
after-election-night-defeat-to-shannon-long/?ipid=topheadlinesmodule-stories)
provided to local media, Johnson congratulated Long and said he respected the
election results.

Long campaigned against Johnson’s hardline tactics and said he would rebuild
trust in the Latino community. During Johnson’s time in office, Latinos more
than doubled their share of the population, from roughly 7 to 16 percent, and
some residents told _Bolts_ in earlier reporting that [they fear
interactions](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-
shannon-long/) with local sheriff’s deputies._ _

On Thursday, Long said his win is a “stop the bleeding” moment for the county.

“It's an opportunity to create change, to increase, to expand, to advance the
public safety here in the county,” Long said.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/20260510_ALAMANCE_BOLTS_109.jpg)Shannon Long won the
sheriff election in Alamance County; here he stands for a portrait near
Burlington in May 9, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Biba for Bolts).

He also pledged to not “do what has been done in the past with ICE,” and said
he would not participate in the 287(g) program.

“I don't see fit to have my officers serve on that side of the law,” he said.

In an earlier interview in May, Long had told _Bolts_ that the 287(g) program,
which has rapidly expanded across the country since Trump took office in
January 2025, is operating with “neglectful policy and procedure,”
specifically related to the racial profiling of Latinos and the targeting of
immigrants who aren’t “high-level criminals.” He also said he would not hold
people for ICE in the county’s detention center outside what’s mandated by
state law.

To alleviate residents’ fears, he wants deputies to be more visible in the
community—“actually getting out of the car and meeting with the residents of
the county.” He said, “We’re going to do our job, and our job is not to do
what they’re doing, which is, right now, racial profiling.”

But it won’t be so easy, advocates say. Mejia told _Bolts_ it’s unclear
whether a new sheriff alone can remedy the fear and distrust that became so
entrenched under the current sheriff.

“When we look at what makes communities safe and what improves well-being,
oftentimes it's not policing,” they said. “It's education, it's food, it’s
third spaces where people can be.”

Long acknowledged that the sheriff doesn’t need to be the face of public
safety, but he thinks he does need a seat at the table. “I do not have to be
the spokesman,” Long said. “I think that’s important, and that’s a part of
giving everybody their voice back.”

Ian Baltutis, a Burlington city council member and the city’s former three-
term mayor, said Long will also have to contend with the sheriff's office
internal power structure, which Johnson cultivated for more than two decades
and could undermine Long’s efforts to rebuild community trust.

“Of anyone who's run for this race, he most clearly understands that
challenge, and is already working to address it,” said Baltutis, a Democrat
who won a seat in the state House on Tuesday as his party scored stunning
upsets and flipped control of the chamber.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/20260510_ALAMANCE_BOLTS_042-e1781624929392.jpg)Shannon
Long talks to a voter at a hot air ballon festival on May 9, 2026. (Photo by
Jacob Biba for Bolts)

Another immediate challenge Long will face is the county’s
[overcrowded](https://alamancenews.com/tempers-flare-as-sheriff-seeks-to-
apply-for-5-6-million-in-state-federal-grants/) detention center, which, [like
many North Carolina
jails](https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/07/20/nc-jail-crowding/),
saw its population surge following enactment of a new state law forcing
harsher pretrial detention rules. Johnson cited the law as the reason [he
ended his agreement to hold ICE
detainees](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/immigration/alamance-
county-terry-johnson-sheriff-ice/), and also said Trump’s mass deportation
plan was straining county resources.

Kristen Powers, executive director of Benevolence Farm, a local nonprofit
supporting formerly incarcerated women and gender expansive people that also
operates a bail fund, said jail conditions and medical care at the facility
are a pressing concern.

“We often bail people out who are in medical crisis and have said, ‘I didn’t
get my diabetes medication or my anti-seizure medication,’” Powers said.

Long, she said, has both an opportunity to address how incarcerated people are
cared for in the county’s jail, but also a chance to use discretion more
strategically when determining whether an individual needs to be jailed,
especially if they have mental health issues.

“I think Sheriff Johnson talked a lot about mental health and getting people
to treatment, and that was like a big thing of his for a long time,” Powers
said. “But I felt there was so much more room to be creative—like, why did
that person even need to be arrested by a police officer in the first place?”
